extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Examination guidance from the MPEP on evaluating secondary considerations (commercial success, long‑felt need, skepticism, copying), enablement/utility/operability issues, attribution affidavits, and file‑wrapper/search recordkeeping requirements during patent prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from specification functions/advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from the functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the description in the specification; success may not be attributable to improvements or modifications made by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be pertinent to nonobviousness, nexus is required between commercial success and the claimed invention (In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc., 752 F.2d 1564). If commercial success is due to features not disclosed or to later modifications, it is not probative. Examples and case citations illustrate limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus especially difficult in design cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In design cases, evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design and not to brand name recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing nexus is especially difficult in design patents; commercial success not accompanied by evidence attributing it to the design is not probative (Litton Systems, Inc. v. Whirlpool Corp.). Examiner should look for evidence directly tying sales to the claimed design rather than other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures alone do not show commercial success absent evidence as to market share, the time period of sales, or what sales would normally be expected in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicants rely on sales figures, provide context (market share, time period, expected sales) or citations (Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish). Uncontextualized gross sales are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need: recognized, persistent, not solved by others
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must satisfy a long‑felt need which was recognized, persistent, and not previously solved by others to be relevant to nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish with objective evidence that an art‑recognized problem existed for a long time without solution. Consider: (1) problem must have been recognized by those of ordinary skill; (2) must not have been satisfied by prior art before the applicant’s invention; (3) the invention must in fact satisfy the need. Cases: In re Gershon; Newell Companies v. Kenney; In re Cavanagh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need measured from date problem identified and efforts made
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze long‑felt need as of the date the problem was identified and efforts were made to solve it, not as of the date of the most pertinent prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the date when the problem was recognized and attempts to solve it were ongoing (Texas Instruments Inc. v. ITC). This affects weighing long‑felt need evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other factors causing failure of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of others to solve a problem may be due to lack of interest or lack of appreciation of marketability rather than lack of technical know‑how; such factors must be considered when weighing long‑felt need/failure of others evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume failure implies difficulty—consider economic/market factors (Scully Signal Co. v. Electronics Corp. of America). Legislative/regulatory contexts and bona fide licensing can affect weight of affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts as evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief or skepticism by experts before inventors proved them wrong constitute strong evidence of nonobviousness and are entitled to fair evidentiary weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony that experts were initially incredulous, particularly when contemporaneous and predating the invention, can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness (Environmental Designs v. Union Oil; In re Dow Chemical; Burlington Industries v. Quigg). Consider duration and contemporaneous nature of skepticism and supporting facts (years of research, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying may show nonobviousness but requires more than mere copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors copied the invention can be presented as secondary evidence of nonobviousness, but more than mere copying is necessary because copying may be due to other factors (lack of concern for patent property, contempt, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying persuasive when an alleged infringer spent substantial time trying and failing to design a similar product and then copied the claimed invention (Dow Chemical v. American Cyanamid). Not persuasive if the copy is not identical or the competitor made little effort (Pentec v. Graphic Controls). Consider duration, effort, and similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should not opine on operability of cited patents; affidavits must rebut presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Since patents are presumed valid (35 U.S.C. 282) and operable, examiners should not express opinions on the operability of a cited patent; affidavits/declarations attacking operability must rebut the presumption by a preponderance of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption that a process disclosed will produce the described product is strong; mere showing of possible operation without the alleged result is insufficient to overcome presumption (Metropolitan Eng. Co. v. Coe; In re Weber). Failures by experimenters with no stake should be given less weight. Where inoperability is asserted as to features not relied upon, other operative features still make the reference effective (In re Shepherd). If a patent teaches/suggests the claimed invention, the patentee’s affidavit that they didn’t intend that use is immaterial (In re Pio).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to require evidence of utility/operability (reference to MPEP §2107)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when it is proper to require evidence of utility or operativeness and how to evaluate submitted evidence is provided (see MPEP §2107.02 and §§2107‑2107.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult the specified MPEP sections for utility examination guidelines and relevant legal precedent when deciding whether to require evidence of utility/operability under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement, burden shifts to applicant to present persuasive arguments supported by proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the disclosure as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence supplementing a specification that appears deficient must show that the missing information would have been known to those of ordinary skill (In re Brandstadter; In re Howarth). Affidavits/declarations are not acceptable to establish facts the specification should recite (In re Buchner). Opinion testimony merely asserting disclosure is insufficient, but opinion testimony that explains underlying factual basis may be admissible and weighed case‑by‑case (Glaser v. Strickland reexamining In re Oppenauer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits/declarations generally not for interpreting disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations purporting merely to explain or interpret the disclosure of a pending application are usually not considered; exceptions exist where testimony explains underlying factual basis for an opinion and is evaluated case‑by‑case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Oppenauer holds such affidavits are usually inadmissible; Glaser v. Strickland qualified the rule under evidentiary standards—opinions that explain factual bases may be helpful if weighed carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution affidavits/declarations to remove references
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances, an affidavit or declaration may attribute an activity or reference to the applicant; if successful, the reference is no longer applicable as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where subject matter disclosed but not claimed in a joint filing is later claimed by one party, an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.132 showing prior invention can overcome the reference (see MPEP §715). Published authorship or patent inventorship does not by itself create a presumption in favor of inventorship for the applicant; applicant must provide satisfactory showing (In re Katz). An unequivocal uncontradicted statement from the applicant can be accepted (In re DeBaun), but contrary evidence can defeat it (Ex parte Kroger; In re Carreira). A successful 1.132 affidavit does not permit assuming the prior reference’s date to defeat later references (In re Costello). Examples provided illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements to disqualify commonly owned U.S. patent/publication (37 CFR 1.130)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disqualify a commonly owned U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication as prior art under 37 CFR 1.130(a), an applicant/owner must submit (1) a terminal disclaimer under §1.321(c) and (2) an oath or declaration stating current common ownership and that the applicant/patentee is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(a) applies where the inventions are not patentably distinct and the cited patent/publication is not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b). The affidavit/declaration must show the inventor named in the application/patent under reexamination invented the subject matter before the reference’s invention, subject to limitations on dates of invention established in NAFTA/WTO rules. 37 CFR 1.130(b) covers double patenting rejections and terminal disclaimers to obviate them. See related MPEP sections for details (§804.03, §706.02(l)).

rubrics_metrics.name: File wrapper contents should be permanent and not withdrawn
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that do not become a permanent part of the record should not be entered on the 'Contents' of the file wrapper. Papers legally entered on the Contents are given a paper number and should not be withdrawn or returned without special authority; certain documents may be returned under 37 CFR 1.59.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.214 may be used to notify applicant that papers ordinarily will not be returned. Certain inadvertently submitted papers or proprietary information not important to patentability may be returned per MPEP §724; some oaths executed abroad may be returned with copies retained in file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of papers in file wrapper
rubrics_metrics.description: Until revision for allowance, specification, amendments and applicant communications are fastened to the left side (center fold) in inverse chronological order; Office actions and communications on the right with drawing print always kept on top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When duplicate amendments are submitted, duplicates are destroyed except when duplicate is received within reply period and original is late—then both placed in file. At allowance, only papers required by the printer are kept in center section. Follow MPEP §608.02(m) for endorsement of prints/sketches with application number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of drawing prints and specimen prints
rubrics_metrics.description: Prints of drawings are fastened inside the file wrapper by OIPE; white paper prints are kept on top of the papers on the right of the file wrapper; prints and inked sketches filed should be endorsed with application number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §608.02(m). Drawing prints management intended for examiner convenience and consistent recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections to file wrapper data must follow procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner notices an error in data on the file wrapper or PALM bib‑data sheet (inventorship, filing date, prior U.S. application numbers, priority claims), the application should be returned to OIPE for correction or routed to technical support staff for PALM correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Office of Initial Patent Examination Data Base Routing Slip with explanation. Examples of corrections: (A) inventorship changes under 37 CFR 1.48; (B) filing date corrections; (C) prior U.S. application number errors; (D) correction of priority claims. Other corrections performed in the TC; assignment name/address errors corrected by Assignment Division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name/residence distinctions and changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'residence' and Post Office address; unless specifically requested by applicant, the residence will not be changed on the file even if a new oath gives a different residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §605.02 and §605.03 for procedures when applicant changes name (MPEP §605.04(c)). Do not change residence on file absent applicant request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification during examination and CLASSIFICATION HISTORY entries
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new application is received, classification and the initials/name of the examiner assigned or docket designation are noted in pencil on the file wrapper and should be kept current; classifiers and examiners who review an application for class assignment should record in the CLASSIFICATION HISTORY box that such review occurred with name/initials, class(es) considered, and date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries are to reduce needless routing and save examiner time. No other information is permitted in the CLASSIFICATION HISTORY box. Consult MPEP §903.07(a) regarding SEARCH NOTES box for consultations involving classification propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index of Claims must be kept up to date
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Index of Claims' in the file wrapper must be kept current as a reliable index of all claims standing in an application and of the amendment in which claims are found. Independent claims should be designated by encircling the claim number in red ink; draw red lines to denote number of claims originally presented and highest numbered claim added by each amendment; annotate rewritten claims with 'Amend. X'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim is canceled, draw a line through its number. Keep space updated showing date and type of Office action and resulting status of each claim. Preprinted claim series refer to original claim numbers; maintain final numbering column for allowed claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Search entries in 'SEARCHED' box
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first action on the merits, the examiner must record classes/subclasses of U.S. and foreign patents, abstract collections, and other sources searched, and the date(s) of the search, in the 'SEARCHED' box; subsequent updates must be endorsed and dated and include databases/search queries/classifications used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search entries printed on patent front page are limited to certain types: (A) complete search of a subclass (record full class/subclass); (B) limited search of a subclass (record class/subclass plus portion searched in parentheses); (C) updates of previously made searches (mark '(updated)' and indicate which search updated). When updating from a parent application, indicate 'updated from parent S.N. ...' or parent patent number. Be precise about places searched and dates; include queries and classifications for updates. See MPEP §904.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'SEARCH NOTES' box entries to complete record (not printed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries in the 'SEARCH NOTES' box are of equal importance to those in the 'SEARCHED' box but are not printed on resulting patents; they are intended to complete the application file record of areas and/or documents considered by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record searches such as partial searches, publication‑only searches, or other searches not qualifying for the printed 'Field of Search' entry in the SEARCHED box. Each search should be dated and initialed. Use the SEARCH NOTES box to provide a complete, accurate, and uniform record of what was searched and considered for each application.
